items.title: George Avakian interviewed by Monk Rowe, Clinton, New York, April 21, 1998
items.q: Marshall encouraged me. He said, “George look, you can do it, you’ve got the texts”... I was in his home almost every Friday night... Marshall not only had a superb record collection but he had an open house every Friday night for anyone who wanted to come and listen to records and talk and exchange

ctx.x: You had mentioned Marshall Stearns as a very important person in your life.

Absolutely. Marshall Stearns was a graduate school student. We all thought he was a college professor because he had a byline that gave 20 Lake Place, New Haven, Connecticut as the place to write to him about questions about jazz and so forth. But to my surprise when I enrolled as a freshman in 1937 I found that he was living just off campus with his wife and going to the graduate school to get a Ph.D. in English Literature. And the great discovery was that Marshall not only had a superb record collection but he…
wanted of course and he asked us to make out the labels, and so that’s how it came about that there are two years worth of labels made out by King and Avakian.

items.title: Avakian George — Smithsonian Jazz Oral History
items.q: Marshall was terrific to us. As I say, every Friday night we were invited. He had what I think had to be one of the best record collections in the world at the time... He made Jerry and me his Brownies – that’s what he called us – to sit down and affix these Dennison labels...

ctx.x: Were the other bands – was it easier for the other bands to be heard because they were white?

Oh yes, definitely. I remember that Ellington was very seldom heard on the radio. All of these black musicians were not heard much. I got into Ellington because of the popular songs that he wrote and recorded. I remember one of the first ones that I ever bought was Sophisticated Lady, on Brunswick. The path led, of course, into other Ellington music. By the time I graduated from Horace Mann, I had quite a few Ellington Brunswicks. items.q: A rock artist manager named John Kennedy ... had a party which was like Marshall Stearn’s Friday nights.

ctx.x: I’ve seen that first hand with my wife and her sister. I’m proud about one thing, that Gloria Steinem once told somebody that George Avakian was the first women’s lib husband, because I supported my wife in her career so thoroughly. I met Gloria Steinem the first time in my own home when Paul Desmond brought her up for dinner on the night that he was going off to London after we had finished an album at RCA with Bob Prince having written string arrangements for settings for Paul’s improvisations. The album was…

There’s a reason beyond Gloria Steinem when I’m going to talk about this. God, these long stories that I get into. But I think they’re interesting. I really do. The other side of that What’s New? album yielded two things for Teo. One was that Leonard Bernstein heard it and liked it so much that he commissioned Teo to write a concerto for six-piece jazz band and symphony orchestra, which he debuted a year later with the New York Philharmonic.
